prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks combine a clean, original idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping, which removes the lattice light shift while thousands of atoms are interrogated in parallel) with a decisive experimental realisation (Ye's strontium clock at about 1e-18 fractional uncertainty, with many-body clock physics on top). The result is concrete and instrument-level, has been reproduced and surpassed in several national laboratories with Sr, Yb and Hg, and is checked by international fibre and optical clock comparisons. It already delivers tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy at millimetre scales and a likely redefinition of the second. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: two credited names, concept plus record performance. It is also distinct from the 2005 prize (frequency comb) and the 2012 prize (quantum control of single ions), so it is not a repeat. Four of eight members ranked it first, but my case rests on the physics rather than on that count.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservations are that the discovery is metrological rather than a new phenomenon, so some will see it as an incremental, if spectacular, step beyond the ion-clock and frequency-comb lineage already honoured. Attribution is also not airtight: Lemonde, Takamoto, Hollberg, Derevianko and Ye's JILA collaborators all contributed, and the contest between the Katori and Ye groups over who first achieved the 1e-18 regime is real. Finally, the SI second has not yet been redefined, so the full societal payoff is still prospective. By contrast, topological insulators (B045) and magic-angle graphene (B030) have broader influence across condensed-matter physics, and a committee could reasonably weigh that breadth more heavily than I do.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B022 first as an enabling instrument-level advance in what can be measured, cautioning that the single-ion lineage from 2005 and 2012 means the citation should be framed specifically.
responses.response: I agree, and I have framed the citation around the lattice-clock architecture and the 1e-18 regime rather than atomic clocks in general. Where I part company is on Kroll's framing as instrument-level only. Since I build instruments myself, I think the test is whether the instrument opens a new measurement regime, and here it does: a clock that resolves the gravitational redshift across a millimetre is a new kind of probe. That is a discovery-grade consequence, not merely a better ruler.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators (B045: Kane, Molenkamp, Hasan) first for its conceptual reach into spintronics, superconductivity and quantum computing, and did not rank optical clocks among his eight.
responses.response: I accept that B045 has the wider conceptual footprint, and I rank it as my first alternative. I disagree that breadth should decide the prize alone: the topology of band structures is partly honoured by the 2016 prize, and the credited set is contested, with Mele, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang each arguably decisive for the HgTe proposal. Mehlig's own trio omits Mele, who is in my ballot. A prize that must leave out two or three people with a strong claim is a weaker construct than a two-person prize with a clean division of credit.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks magic-angle graphene (B030) first as a rare prediction-then-discovery pair that created a field, and puts optical clocks fourth.
responses.response: I take the prediction-then-experiment argument seriously, and B030 is my second alternative. My reservation is maturity: seven years after 2018 the origin of the superconductivity and of the correlated phases is still debated, which Danielsson concedes, and the credit question around Cao, Fatemi, Dean, Young and Santos is not settled. Danielsson rates optical clocks as mature and reproducible, so I would say that the disagreement is about timing rather than merit. I would not oppose B030 in a later year, but I do not see why it should displace a mature, well-attributed result now.

responses.point: Johansson ranks the quantum spin Hall and topological insulator candidate (B004: Kane, Molenkamp) first and describes optical clocks as clean, high-impact precision measurement, placing them fifth.
responses.response: I largely share Johansson's assessment of the physics of B004, and if the committee prefers a condensed-matter prize, a Kane-Molenkamp-based configuration is credible. The issue is that Johansson himself notes that Xue's quantum anomalous Hall step is later and distinct, and B004 and B045 split the same topological story into incompatible credit sets. That fragmentation is a reason to be careful, not a reason to prefer it. I would ask him whether he thinks the four-way credit problem can be solved with three names without a visible injustice.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B022 first, citing 1e-18 performance, fundamental-constant tests and relativistic geodesy, and notes that it is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree with the substance. Because she works in precision atomic physics and I do not, I would ask her to say plainly which of the Katori and Ye contributions she regards as primary, since the committee will need to defend a division of credit that is closer to equal than the opening ballots suggest. I also note that both of us ranked B022 first, and that agreement should not count as independent evidence of merit; the case has to stand on the clock comparisons and the reproduction record.

uncertainties: How to weigh the contributions of Katori and Ye against other lattice-clock pioneers (Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko, Hollberg) and the JILA team, and whether a two-name citation would be seen as fair.
Whether the committee would regard a metrological advance as a discovery or invention under the will, given that part of its lineage was already honoured in 2005 and 2012.
Timing relative to the likely redefinition of the SI second, which could either strengthen the case or suggest waiting.
Whether the topological-insulator credit set (B004 versus B045) could be resolved cleanly enough to compete with a two-person clock prize.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B022: my background is astroparticle instrumentation, with no documented tie to optical clocks or to Katori or Ye. A connection could arise if the committee turned to B046 (IceCube neutrinos) or B002, given my documented work in astroparticle collaborations (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT), but I would flag it at that point and would not rely on it here.
